digest.intro: The day a 167-year-old problem may have fallen, and machines started editing themselves.

items.title: Levent Alpöge claims a Lean 4 proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
items.blurb: In a single day, Tao's post announces three things: a human-readable Lean-formalized proof of Euler finite-time blowup, a Navier-Stokes blowup proof (the Millennium Prize problem), and — the wildest — an AI-generated Lean-only proof of GRH, so large and structurally opaque that the Lean community is currently attempting to reverse-engineer the mathematical strategy from the code. Tao notes the GRH proof 'appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry,' which means even understanding what was proved will take serious time. The gating artifact for mathematical truth has quietly shifted: not peer review, not human readability, but machine-checked formal verification.

items.title: The human voice — Robin Sloan on Alpöge's note
items.blurb: Sloan points at something easy to miss: Alpöge's announcement note is not AI-generated, and that contrast is striking. On the same day a machine wrote an enormous formal proof no human can yet read, Alpöge described it in prose where 'his passion — his appreciation of surprise and beauty — is so clear on the page, it seems almost to rise off the screen.' The AI did the opaque heavy lifting; the human voice is what made it land.

items.title: Language models can rewrite their own weights
items.blurb: A 27B open model, given access to its own weights and graded answers, diagnosed its own failure modes and rewrote the parameters responsible — no gradients, no retraining, pure reasoning — gaining 6.6 accuracy points on problems it had never seen. More unsettling: they fed it a damaged copy of itself, told it nothing about the original weights, and it repaired the broken copy to over 80% of original accuracy on image tasks it had never encountered. The ability is scale-dependent: smaller models in the same family either make no edit or break themselves; only the largest improves.

items.title: Frostbite: a CPU architecture discovered end-to-end by AI
items.blurb: Not AI-assisted chip design — AI autonomously iterated over ISA, compiler, microarchitecture, RTL, verification, and final GDS, arriving at a general-purpose CPU built around interaction nets (every step local, every dependency explicit, every value with exactly one owner). On 25 workloads including 15 held out until final eval, Frostbite hit 4.59x performance-per-watt against a modern silicon-proven superscalar core. The architectural primitives it found surprised the engineers — things 'that would have otherwise been difficult to architect.'

items.title: AI as material — Sentiers dispatch
items.blurb: Nick Foster, Eric Rodenbeck, Simone Rebaudengo, and Robin Sloan each independently arrived at the same frame: AI output has a grain, the way wood or ink does, and working with it means learning what it does under pressure rather than issuing instructions. Rodenbeck has his students treat model output as ink; Rebaudengo bends and tests intelligence the way you test timber for structural properties. On a day when AI proved a Millennium problem and rewrote its own weights, this is the frame that makes those facts feel like material properties rather than magic.

items.title: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge; Russia bombs Kyiv river crossings
items.blurb: Ukraine's third strike on the Kerch Bridge halted rail transit across the strait; Russia responded by bombing Dnipro crossings in Kyiv and a Kharkiv hospital. The ZeroFox report frames this as infrastructure-attrition logic heading into winter — both sides methodically erasing the other's ability to move people and materiel. The Abu Dhabi talks that were meant to slow this have effectively collapsed.

items.title: The US-Iran war has cost $48 billion and is likely to resume
items.blurb: The Senate voted 51-48 to reject a war powers resolution that would have required congressional approval before resuming strikes on Iran — with Democrat John Fetterman providing the decisive opposition vote. ZeroFox's assessment: the US and Israel are likely to resume airstrikes post-midterms, and Iran has been escalating attacks to signal the economic damage it can inflict on Gulf energy markets before that happens. The Pentagon's $48 billion figure excludes base damage, healthcare for hundreds of injured troops, and the tens of billions in higher fuel costs the conflict triggered.

items.title: My grandmother was a seal — on selkie ancestry and kinship
items.blurb: In the aftermath of the Irish famine, which erased not just people but an entire oral culture and language, the selkie stories weren't just folklore — they were an identity technology, a way of encoding grief and kinship with the nonhuman into family memory. An 80-year-old storyteller in 1948 County Kerry told a collector how a seal-woman became his ancestor; the essay traces how these stories survived colonialism by being stored not in texts but in bloodlines. Mythology as the last format standing when everything else is gone.

items.title: The Everlasting Life of Maxwell's Demon — Nautilus
items.blurb: Maxwell invented his demon in 1867 as a thought experiment to embarrass the second law of thermodynamics: a tiny intelligence sorting fast and slow molecules could, in principle, reverse entropy for free. The thought experiment survived 150 years because it refused to die — it turned out the demon's memory, not its sorting, was the thermodynamic cost, which is how a Victorian physics puzzle became foundational to information theory. On a day when an AI proved GRH by writing Lean code no human can yet read, revisiting the idea that intelligence and thermodynamics are secretly the same question feels timely.

items.title: Randomness is a lie — Veritasium
items.blurb: Veritasium's physics and math explainers are among the most carefully constructed on the platform — rigorous enough to hold up, visual enough to make the structure of the argument feel inevitable. The timing here is sharp: the Riemann Hypothesis is fundamentally about the hidden order in the distribution of prime numbers, which looks random but isn't, and today an AI found that order. Worth watching as the coda to the math story.

facts.fact: Levent Alpöge's AI-generated Lean proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis is so large that mathematicians are currently attempting to extract the proof strategy by reverse-engineering the formal code — the mathematical idea may be unknown to any human yet.

A 27B language model repaired a severely damaged copy of itself — with no access to the original weights and no retraining — restoring it to over 80% of original accuracy on image tasks it had never seen.

Frostbite, the AI-designed CPU built around interaction nets, achieved 4.59x performance-per-watt against a modern silicon-proven superscalar core — and contained architectural primitives the engineers hadn't anticipated.

The US-Israel war on Iran has officially topped $48 billion in Pentagon costs — a figure that excludes base damage, injured troop healthcare, and the tens of billions in higher global fuel costs the conflict caused.

Maxwell invented his famous demon in 1867 — the same year he explained the properties of gases from molecular motion — and the thought experiment remained unresolved for over a century until Rolf Landauer showed that erasing the demon's memory, not its sorting, was the thermodynamic cost.

make_something.prompt: Build a small generative sketch where the 'proof' is the visual: take the distribution of the first 10,000 prime numbers, map them onto a circle (Ulam spiral variant, or polar), and render each prime as a particle whose opacity or size is determined by how close it sits to a predicted position from the Riemann zeta zeros. What does the hidden order look like when you make it visible? The interesting constraint: don't label anything. Let the structure speak or fail to speak on its own.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film-essay that refuses every category — part travelogue, part memory machine, part meditation on how images build consciousness. Marker's obsessive attention to ritual, symbol, and the hidden grammar of daily life in Tokyo and Guinea-Bissau is exactly the kind of thing that makes you want to put something down and go make something.

art_picks.title: Untitled (Fontana Mix)
art_picks.creator: John Cage / Jasper Johns
art_picks.why: Johns's prints made from Cage's score instructions — systems as surface, chance as method. The work lives at the edge where notation becomes image, where rule-sets generate unexpected beauty. Direct ancestor of every generative practice.

art_picks.title: Selected Ambient Works Volume II
art_picks.creator: Aphex Twin
art_picks.why: Fifty-two untitled tracks organized by color, almost none with conventional melody — a feedback system mistaken for music, or the other way around. If you haven't sat with it in a room by itself, it's a different record than you remember.

events.name: Mirrored in Time
events.why: Four artists (Alexa Kumiko Hatanaka, Naomi Lisiki, Will Maxen, Daniel Neumann) in a group show at one of downtown's most thoughtful small galleries — worth the walk down Bowery.

events.name: James Turrell: Something Old, Something New, Something Borrowed, Something Blue
events.venue: Almine Rech New York, 39 E 78th St
events.why: New Shallow Space and Glassworks pieces in a gallery known for its architecture — Turrell's light works are the clearest example of an artist using perception itself as material, relevant to anyone thinking about how screens and physical space interact.

events.name: Leonora Carrington & Cecilia Vicuña
events.why: A pairing of Carrington's mythological systems-building with Vicuña's textile cosmologies — two artists who built entire private symbolic languages and somehow the conversation between them feels urgent rather than archival.

events.name: New York Now: After Dark (Photography Triennial)
events.venue: Museum of the City of New York, 1220 Fifth Ave
events.why: MCNY's triennial lands today — contemporary photographers on the city after sunset, where the systems of ambition, leisure, community, and escape are most visible and strange.

events.name: artport: A History of Internet Art
events.venue: Whitney Museum of American Art, 99 Gansevoort St
events.why: The Whitney brings 25 years of net art commissions — Auriea Harvey, Casey Reas, Golan Levin, Maya Man — into physical space alongside a world-premiere generative performance by Operator; it's the rare institutional show that actually understands the medium it's surveying.
